articles.title: Jaguar's 'ambitious' Type 01 EV arrives after controversial rebrand — and in a challenging marketplace
articles.summary: Jaguar has a lot riding on its new Type 01 all-electric sedan.
articles.body:
Jaguar has a lot riding on its new vehicle, the Type 01.

Revealed last night in New York, the new EV sedan is the production version of the Type 00 concept. It retains the hard angles, dramatic long hood, and truncated rear end of the concept, but with slightly normalized proportions.

The conversion to a sedan also makes it more palatable to a broader subset of buyers compared to the concept's coupe design. Inside the cabin is another story, with a "brass floating spine" bisecting the interior and bucket-type seating in the back, creating a four-seat grand tourer.

The specs are impressive, and like most EVs, it boasts abundant power. Jaguar said the swooping sedan will pump out 1,016 hp, hit 0 to 62mph in 3.2 seconds, and have an estimated range of 450 miles.

Reviews of the design are mixed, but in the auto world, that's expected. It will likely appeal to a certain luxury buyer looking to stand out from the crowd, starting with its $130,000-and-up price tag. Jaguar said it will sell fewer cars and target more affluent customers when deliveries of the Type 01 begin next year.

"This is the toughest possible segment to stake your company's future on. The market for luxury EVs is soft," said Rory Caroll, editorial director of Alloy , a car culture publication. "But the Type 01 has real presence, it's ambitious, kind of a car for the future we wanted but didn't get. It's expensive, but less so than other hyperluxury EVs."

The big question: Will those buyers turn up for Jaguar? It was only two years ago that the controversial "Copy Nothing" marketing campaign was unleashed, with models strutting out in avant-garde outfits. It was pilloried by some on social media as out of touch, or even "woke." The ad didn't include a car in the video either.

Then a Barbie Pink version of the concept debuted shortly thereafter, and the criticism remained. Jaguar design boss Gerry McGovern departed the company a few weeks after the reveal, and CEO Adrian Mardell left a few months after that.

This comes after the company killed off its existing products — including well-received but long-in-the-tooth SUVs — to focus on its EV reboot. This only adds to the challenge facing Jaguar.

Then there's the fact that the company had to dig itself out of a PR hole just to get to where it is today.

"Jaguar has had a remarkable half-year for a brand with nothing on sale," said Royan Boulter, mobility lead at PR measurement firm CARMA, noting there have been more than 400 articles about the car before it was even revealed.

articles.title: US mortgage rates hit their highest level in three years
articles.summary: Rising borrowing costs have pushed mortgage applications to their lowest level since February 2025.
articles.body:
Mortgage rates in the United States have hit their highest level in nearly three years, as cost-of-living concerns weigh on Americans less than a month before the midterm elections.

The average cost for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped 19 basis points to 7.49 percent for the week ending October 2 , according to the Mortgage Bankers Association’s weekly report released on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, applications for mortgages tumbled 4.2 percent from the previous week, according to the report. Applications are at their lowest level since February 2025 and have fallen by almost half since the beginning of the year.

“Very few homeowners have an incentive to refinance at these rates, and the jump in borrowing costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase market,” Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, said in a press release.

Mortgage rates are closely tied to US 10-year Treasury notes. Earlier this week, those hit a 24-year high of 5.3 percent amid surging oil prices tied to ongoing tensions with Iran.

Meanwhile, the yield on 30-year Treasury bonds rose to its highest level since 2002, at 5.7 percent on Wednesday.

Mortgage rates have jumped since late February, when the US and Israel first struck Iran. Since the strikes, mortgage rates have climbed 1.4 percent. Inflation, which has risen by 3.4 percent from a year ago, is also putting pressure on mortgage rates.

It comes as the cost of living is top of mind for voters as they approach the congressional midterm elections that could decide the balance of power in Washington, DC. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll in late August, 47 percent of voters said that the cost of living was the single most important issue ahead of the midterms.

In a separate Reuters/Ipsos poll in September, 17 percent of voters said they approved of US President Donald Trump’s handling of cost of living-related issues.

articles.title: As mortgage rates rise, more borrowers are turning to adjustable-rate loans
articles.summary: Nearly 11% of borrowers who locked in a rate in mid-September opted for an adjustable-rate mortgage.
articles.body:
As mortgage rates approach 8%, more buyers are turning to adjustable-rate mortgages to save on interest.

Nearly 11% of mortgage borrowers who locked in a rate in mid-September opted for an ARM, according to ICE Mortgage Technology data. The share is up more than three percentage points over the past three months to the highest in nearly four years.

ARMs can offer meaningful rate savings over a 30-year fixed-rate loan, but there's a catch: Instead of locking in one rate for the entire 30-year term, borrowers commit to an initial, often lower rate for a shorter period, typically five or seven years. After the initial term is up, their rate adjusts based on market conditions once or twice a year.

In the chart above, "rate lock activity" refers to borrowers locking in a rate after applying for a mortgage. Refinancings are leading the trend, likely driven by owners who took out a fixed-rate loan above 7% and those needing to cash out some of their equity.

Many borrowers think the rate gamble is worth i t : While the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is around 7.63% on Wednesday, a 7/6 ARM — which carries a fixed term for seven years and then adjusts every six months — is 6.95%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Many borrowers who seek out ARMs intend to sell their home before their initial fixed-rate term expires. Others are effectively betting that rates will be lower in the future, allowing them to refinance.

Most borrowers who took out ARMs in 2022 and 2023, when rates first started moving higher, remain in their initial fixed-rate period, meaning the Fed's recent tightening hasn't affected their rates. While 30-year fixed mortgage rates aren't directly influenced by the Fed, ARMs in their adjustment rates are much more sensitive to the central bank's interest rate decisions.

Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.
